subsystems.name: Neural signal acquisition
subsystems.role: records the electrical activity the key will be derived from.
parts: scalp electrodes or an implanted microelectrode array
shielding from mains and muscle noise

subsystems.name: Challenge protocol
subsystems.role: presents a repeatable stimulus or mental task so the brain produces a comparable response each time.

subsystems.name: Feature extraction
subsystems.role: turns raw waveforms into numbers that are stable for one person and different between people.
parts: evoked-response components such as the P300

subsystems.name: Key derivation core
subsystems.role: converts a noisy biometric reading into an exactly reproducible cryptographic key.
parts: key-derivation function and hash (e.g. SHA-3, HKDF)

subsystems.name: Protected template store
subsystems.role: keeps the enrolment reference without storing a usable brainprint.

subsystems.name: Liveness and anti-spoofing
subsystems.role: checks a live, willing person is present rather than a recording or a coerced user.

buildSteps.title: Choose the signal source
buildSteps.detail: Decide between scalp electroencephalography (safe, cheap, noisy) and an implanted array (stable, high-bandwidth, requires surgery). This choice limits everything downstream.

buildSteps.title: Build a recording rig
buildSteps.detail: Use shielded, low-noise amplification and precise stimulus timing, because the features being hashed are microvolt-scale and timing-sensitive.

buildSteps.title: Design the challenge
buildSteps.detail: Pick a task that reliably evokes a subject-specific response — for example an oddball stimulus producing a P300 wave, or imagined movement — and randomise it so it cannot be recorded and replayed.

buildSteps.title: Collect enrolment data
buildSteps.detail: Record the same person across several sessions, days apart, to measure how much their own signal drifts (electrode placement, alertness, caffeine).

buildSteps.title: Select stable features
buildSteps.detail: Keep only features that vary little within a person and a lot between people, discarding the rest; this is the difference between identification research and key generation.

buildSteps.title: Apply error correction
buildSteps.detail: A key must come out bit-for-bit identical every time, so a fuzzy extractor uses an error-correcting code plus helper data to absorb the natural variation in each reading.

buildSteps.title: Derive and bind the key
buildSteps.detail: Hash the corrected feature vector into a key and use it to unlock a disk, credential or hardware secure element. No raw brain data is stored with the ciphertext.

buildSteps.title: Test against attacks
buildSteps.detail: Measure false-accept and false-reject rates, then attempt spoofing with recorded signals, cross-subject substitution, and coercion scenarios.

prerequisites.why: commercial headsets exist, but scalp signals blur millions of neurons together and carry far less detail than the tile's wording implies — they reflect summed field potentials, not individual synaptic firings.
academic studies show EEG can identify individuals, but accuracy falls across sessions and electrode placements.
clinical trials show richer, more stable signals, but they need surgery and long-term biocompatibility.
the mathematics of turning an inexact reading into an exact key is established for fingerprints and iris, though brain signals are noisier.
nothing reliably distinguishes a live, consenting brain from a high-quality recording or a coerced user.
tamper-resistant elements to hold or wrap the derived key are a mature technology.

pathway.milestone: laboratory studies using EEG for identification, not key generation
pathway.unlocks: evidence that a brainprint is distinctive enough to be worth using.

pathway.milestone: error-corrected key derivation demonstrated over repeated sessions in small cohorts
pathway.unlocks: the first genuine brain-derived cryptographic keys, still with a fallback login.

pathway.milestone: multi-modal systems pairing neural signals with another biometric and a liveness challenge
pathway.unlocks: resistance to replay and coercion, enough for high-security access control.

pathway.milestone: routine use of implanted interfaces in medicine
pathway.unlocks: a plausible path to practical neural keys — but the unsolved problem is revocation, since unlike a password or a fingerprint, a person's neural signature cannot be changed if it leaks.
